query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a compositionally complex high-entropy alloy (HEA) that starts as a single-phase material, localized deformation under service-relevant conditions induces dynamic amorphization at grain boundaries. This process leads to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous interfacial layer that acts as a brittle mediator, suppressing the normally ductile behavior by concentrating strain and facilitating crack initiation.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase, compositionally complex HEA (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) with a relatively uniform grain size and no pre-existing brittle intermetallic phases.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled mechanical loading (e.g., high-strain-rate deformation tests and/or cyclic fatigue) under service-relevant conditions (varying temperatures including low temperature) designed to trigger dynamic shear events.
generation.conditions: Tests should cover a range of strain rates and temperatures (especially lower temperatures where dislocation mobility is reduced) to stress the grain boundaries and probe the onset of dynamic amorphization, with comparisons to equivalent treatments on conventional alloys lacking this dynamic mechanism.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultra-nanocrystalline (or amorphous) layer formed by deformation-induced dynamic amorphization at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Under high-strain or low-temperature loading, in the absence of deleterious intermetallic precipitation, the HEA undergoes dynamic amorphization at grain boundaries. This transformation reduces the capacity for dislocation-mediated plasticity, localizes strain and embrittles the boundaries, and thus triggers a loss of toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline ductile behavior of the homogeneous single-phase microstructure, the formation of a brittle, ultra-nanocrystalline boundary region will correlate with an observed reduction in toughness (manifested as earlier crack initiation and propagation) during high-strain-rate and/or low-temperature tests. In contrast, conventional alloys would typically degrade toughness via grain-boundary segregation or precipitate formation rather than by dynamic amorphization.
generation.baseline: Initial single-phase HEA microstructure exhibiting conventional dislocation plasticity and moderate toughness under similar loading conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to be most relevant under high mechanical strain rate and low-temperature conditions where dynamic shear transformation dominates. Under conditions with slower strain rates or elevated temperatures that promote recovery, the deleterious amorphous layer may not form, limiting the effect.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical conditions (strain rate, temperature, and stress level) at which dynamic amorphization transitions from beneficial grain refining to a brittle phase are not fully quantified. There is also some uncertainty regarding the uniformity of this effect across different HEA compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several samples of the same single-phase HEA and a conventional alloy with similar starting microstructure. Subject both materials to a series of mechanical tests (e.g., high-strain-rate uniaxial tension/compression and cyclic fatigue) at multiple temperatures (including low temperatures). Use in situ or post-mortem high-resolution microscopy (e.g., STEM or TEM) to monitor grain-boundary structure and identify any formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous phase.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tests show that toughness degradation in the HEA occurs without the formation of any ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous boundary layer (i.e., if failure characteristics are similar to conventional segregation-induced embrittlement or if ductility remains high despite the loading conditions), then the hypothesis that dynamic amorphization mediates brittle behavior would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
